kurals.tamil:
காமம் உழந்து வருந்தினார்க்கு ஏமம்
மடலல்லது இல்லை வலி.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamam uzhandhu varundhinaarkku Emam
madalalladhu illai vali.
kurals.meaning: For those who have known love and now suffer because it is denied them, there is no protection and no strength left except riding the palm-stem horse (madal) in public.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a boy who has asked and asked for something important and been told no every time. At last he decides to make a big, brave sign and carry it through the whole village so everyone knows how much it matters to him. In old Tamil stories, a young man who was kept away from the girl he loved could do something like this: ride a pretend horse made of palm leaves down the street.
kurals.university: Chapter 114 opens with the custom of madal ūrtal (மடல் ஊர்தல்): a lover refused access to his beloved would ride a hobby-horse made of palmyra stems (madal) through the streets, garlanded with erukkam flowers and carrying her likeness, to shame her family publicly into consenting; Kalittokai and Tolkāppiyam know the practice, and the grammatical tradition classes it as an extreme of love (peruntiṇai). Ēmam (ஏமம்) means 'safeguard, refuge' and vali (வலி) 'strength, support'; uḻantu (உழந்து) is 'having laboured/suffered in'. In the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar the opening couplets are the hero's words to the heroine's confidante (tōḻi) when she puts him off, and the threat of the madal is itself a way of abandoning nāṇ (நாண், 'shame, reserve'), which gives the chapter its name. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss the line as 'no strength but the madal'; Pope renders 'Except the helpful horse of palm, no other strength remains.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Sanskrit dramatic theory lists the stages through which love in separation passes, from longing and anxious thought, through sleeplessness, raving and wasting, to the brink of death.
hinduism.explanation: The Natyashastra treats love denied (vipralambha) as a progressive illness with named stages that actors must be able to portray.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural's lover speaks from deep inside that sickness, where ordinary remedies have failed and only a desperate public act seems left.
hinduism.source: Bharata, Natyashastra, section on the stages of love (kama-avasthas) (paraphrase; tr. Manomohan Ghosh)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory of a well-known list, not checked word for word this session; it matches the lover's condition but has no equivalent of the madal itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved in the Song of Songs calls herself love-sick and begs for something to sustain her.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's sufferer, she treats love as an affliction that leaves her looking for any support at all.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; shares the 'love as sickness needing a remedy' idea, but the remedy asked for is gentle comfort, not a public protest.

islam.quote_or_event: In the Arabic and Persian tale of Layla and Majnun, the young Qays is kept from Layla by her family and is so consumed by love that he is called majnun, 'madman', and goes out into the wilderness reciting verses about her.
islam.explanation: The story, retold by Nizami Ganjavi in 1188, became the classic Islamicate picture of love that has no remedy and no shame left.
islam.tie_back: Majnun, like the Kural's lover, is refused by the beloved's family and lets his suffering become a public spectacle because nothing else is left to him.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known narrative; a strong parallel in situation, though literary rather than scriptural and without the madal's purpose of pressuring the family.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The Song of Songs describes love as a force as unstoppable as death itself.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover has found love just that strong: it has overpowered every defence but one.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; captures the overwhelming force of love but not the specific desperation of a rejected suitor.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From lust springs grief, from lust springs fear. For one who is wholly free from craving there is no grief; whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to desire and teaches that the only lasting cure is freedom from craving.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's sufferer seeks a remedy in the madal; Buddhism diagnoses the same pain but locates the cure in letting the desire go.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; same diagnosis of love-pain, opposite remedy.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Princess Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, is left grief-stricken when he abandons the wedding to become a monk.
jainism.tie_back: She suffers the same pain of love denied as the Kural's lover, but in the Jain story the way out is renunciation, not a public protest.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's diacritics simplified); a genuine Jain story of love-grief, though its resolution runs opposite to the madal.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid, the nymph Echo is rejected by Narcissus, hides herself in the woods in shame, and wastes away with grief until only her voice is left.
greek_mythology.explanation: Echo's unreturned love leaves her with no remedy at all, and it consumes her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She shows the danger the Kural's lover feels: love refused, with no ordinary way to relieve it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; shares the theme of hopeless love, but Echo withdraws in shame where the Kural's lover goes public.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Pascal writes that the heart has its reasons which reason does not know.
philosophy.explanation: For Pascal, love moves by a logic of its own that rational calculation cannot govern.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover has passed beyond calculation; his heart's 'reason' tells him only the madal is left.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Famous line given as paraphrase because the translation was not checked this session; a general thematic fit only.

kurals.tamil:
நோனா உடம்பும் உயிரும் மடலேறும்
நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Nonaa udambum uyirum madalaerum
naaninai neekki niruththu.
kurals.meaning: My body and my life, unable to bear this any longer, have put shame aside and are ready to mount the palm-stem horse.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been so upset that you cried in front of everyone, even though you usually would feel shy? The speaker here says his whole body and heart are hurting so much that his shyness has simply been set aside.
kurals.university: Nōṉā (நோனா) is the negative participle of nōl, 'to endure': the body and the life-breath (uyir) that 'cannot bear' the separation are made the subjects of the verb, as if they act on their own. Nāṇiṉai nīkki niṟuttu (நாணினை நீக்கி நிறுத்து), 'having removed and set aside shame', is the key phrase of the chapter: nāṇ, the sense of reserve that Tamil ethics praises (cf. chapter 102, Nāṇuṭaimai), is not destroyed but deliberately put to one side. Commentators in Parimelazhagar's line take this as the hero telling the confidante that his resolve is already made; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'my body and life have resolved to ride the madal, having set shame aside', while Pappaiah softens it to 'are thinking of riding'. Pope: 'My body and my soul, that can no more endure, / Will lay reserve aside, and mount the horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna plays his flute on the autumn night, the cowherd women of Vraja drop whatever they are doing, leave husbands and households, and run to him in the forest, heedless of what anyone will say.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana presents the gopis' abandonment of social propriety as the highest form of devotion.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, the gopis set aside shame and reserve because love has become unbearable.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a strong fit for love overriding modesty, though in a devotional rather than purely human register.

christianity.quote_or_event: A woman known in the town as a sinner enters a Pharisee's house where Jesus is dining, weeps over his feet, wipes them with her hair, and anoints them, ignoring the disapproval of everyone present.
christianity.explanation: Jesus defends her, saying her many sins are forgiven because she loved much.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, she lets love overrule every rule of decorum in front of onlookers.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the episode; the abandonment of decorum fits, but the love is penitent devotion, not romantic longing.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens his Masnavi by saying that only one whose garment has been torn by a mighty love is cleansed of greed and every fault.
islam.explanation: For Rumi, being 'torn' by love is a purifying loss of self-protection.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's lover is similarly 'torn open': his reserve has been stripped away by love too strong to bear.
islam.source: Jalal al-Din Rumi, Masnavi I.22 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.A. Nicholson)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, wording not verified this session; Rumi's love is mystical, but the image of love stripping away one's covering matches the couplet.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud tells that Rachel, daughter of the wealthy Ben Kalba Savua, chose the poor shepherd Akiva against her father's wishes, and her father vowed she would receive nothing from his property.
judaism.explanation: Rachel gave up wealth, status and family approval for the man she loved and believed in.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, she set aside what society expected of her because her love would not let her do otherwise.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 62b-63a (paraphrase; William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: The story's later part was read on Sefaria this session; this opening summary is paraphrased, and her choice is quiet resolve rather than public display.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Nanda, the Buddha's half-brother, ordained on the day of his wedding, tells the monks he is discontented and wants to return to lay life because he keeps remembering his beautiful fiancée's parting words.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha then leads him to a higher understanding, and Nanda eventually becomes an arahant.
buddhism.tie_back: Nanda's longing, like the Kural lover's, is strong enough to make him ready to throw off the role he is expected to keep.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the canonical episode; the longing fits closely, though Buddhism resolves it by overcoming desire.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When Râgîmatî perceived that Rathanêmi's strength of will was broken, and temptation had got the better of him, she did not lose her presence of mind and defended her Self on that occasion.”
jainism.explanation: The monk Rathanemi, seeing Rajimati in a cave, loses his composure and proposes to her; she keeps hers.
jainism.tie_back: Rathanemi is in the Kural lover's state, with restraint overpowered, and the Jain text sets beside him a figure who refuses to let go of hers.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); describes restraint giving way to desire, which the Jain text then corrects.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes how, at the sight of the beloved, her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, her ears roar, and she trembles until she seems close to death.
greek_mythology.explanation: Her famous poem lists the physical collapse that love brings about in the body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural likewise says it is the body and the life-breath that can no longer bear love and so throw off restraint.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the well-known fragment; close on body and life overpowered, though Sappho says nothing of abandoning shame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Hume argues that reason alone can never oppose a passion in directing the will, and that reason is and ought only to be the slave of the passions.
philosophy.explanation: For Hume, feeling, not reason, ultimately moves us to act.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover is a living example: his considered sense of shame has been simply overruled by passion.
philosophy.source: David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature 2.3.3 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not checked word for word this session; a general philosophical fit.

kurals.tamil:
நாணொடு நல்லாண்மை பண்டுடையேன் இன்றுடையேன்
காமுற்றார் ஏறும் மடல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Naanodu nallaanmai pandudaiyaen indrudaiyaen
kaamutraar aerum madal.
kurals.meaning: Once I had modesty and honourable manliness; today all I have is the palm-stem horse that love-stricken men ride.
kurals.elementary: Think of a proud, well-behaved prince who always acted with dignity. Then he falls so deeply in love that he will do anything, even something silly in front of everyone, to be heard. He says, 'I used to be so proper; now look at me!'
kurals.university: The couplet sets paṇṭu (பண்டு, 'formerly') against iṉṟu (இன்று, 'today'), and nāṇ (நாண், 'modesty, sense of shame') together with nal-āṇmai (நல்லாண்மை, 'good manliness, honourable valour') against the single possession now left, the madal. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads this as the hero's lament that love has stripped him of the two qualities that defined him socially. Kāmuṟṟār (காமுற்றார்) is 'those seized by love'; the madal is thus marked as the emblem of a class of sufferers rather than a personal eccentricity. Pope: 'I once retained reserve and seemly manliness; / To-day I nought possess but lovers' horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's play, King Pururavas, maddened by the loss of the nymph Urvashi, wanders the forest asking a peacock, a cuckoo, a swan, a bee and even a mountain whether they have seen her.
hinduism.explanation: The great king forgets his royal dignity entirely in his grief and longing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Pururavas once had kingly honour and self-command, and now has only the open madness of love.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known act; a close fit for a man of rank losing his dignity to love.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul writes that whatever he once counted as gain, his status, lineage and reputation, he now counts as loss for the sake of Christ.
christianity.explanation: Paul describes giving up everything that once defined his honour for the one he loves above all.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's lover makes the same before-and-after reckoning: his old honour is gone, exchanged for love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the before-and-after structure matches, but Paul speaks of devotion to Christ, not romantic love.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi was a respected jurist and preacher in Konya until his meeting with the wandering dervish Shams of Tabriz; afterwards he gave himself to ecstatic poetry and whirling, to the scandal of many of his followers.
islam.explanation: The hagiographic tradition tells how love for Shams overturned Rumi's dignified public role.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Rumi once had standing and reserve, and love left him with nothing but its open display.
islam.source: Shams al-Din Aflaki, Manaqib al-'Arifin (paraphrase of the traditional account)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a hagiographic tradition not checked this session; the love is spiritual friendship, not romance.

judaism.quote_or_event: Samson, the mighty judge of Israel, reveals the secret of his strength to Delilah because of her persistent pleading; his hair is cut and his strength leaves him.
judaism.explanation: The strongest man in Israel loses the very quality that defined him through his attachment to a woman.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover likewise laments that the 'good manliness' he once had has been taken from him by love.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the biblical narrative; a clear case of manliness lost to love, though the Bible frames it as betrayal rather than longing.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Kusa Jataka, Prince Kusa, rejected by his bride Pabhavati, follows her to her father's kingdom and takes work as a potter, a basket-maker, a gardener and a cook, all to be near her.
buddhism.explanation: The Bodhisatta in this birth story lays aside royal dignity entirely for love.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Kusa once had a prince's honour and now has only the humble tasks love has driven him to.
buddhism.source: Kusa Jataka (Jataka 531) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jataka; a strong narrative parallel for loss of rank and reserve through love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Having heard these well-spoken words of the virtuous lady, he returned to the Law like an elephant driven by the hook.”
jainism.explanation: Rathanemi, rebuked by Rajimati, recovers the self-control his passion had made him lose.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover says he once had reserve and now has only the madal; the Jain story shows the reverse path, from passion back to restraint.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a mirror-image of the Kural's movement rather than a parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Deianira reproaches Heracles that the hero who conquered monsters now sits among serving-women spinning wool for the Lydian queen Omphale, wearing her clothes while she carries his club and lion-skin.
greek_mythology.explanation: The greatest of heroes lays aside his manly identity for love of Omphale.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is exactly the Kural's lament: 'nallāṇmai' (honourable manliness) once possessed, now given up for love.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a close match for manliness surrendered to love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “A man should allow himself to behave as lovers commonly do to their favorites—pressing their suit with supplications and entreaties, binding themselves with vows, sleeping on doorsteps, and submitting to such slavery as no slave would ever endure.”
philosophy.explanation: Pausanias notes that conduct which would bring sharp reproach in any other cause is tolerated in a lover.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover, like Plato's, is reduced to acts that would shame him in any other cause.
philosophy.source: Plato, Symposium 183a (tr. W.R.M. Lamb, via Perseus)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Perseus (sentence lightly trimmed at the start); a close fit for honour given up in love.

kurals.tamil:
காமக் கடும்புனல் உய்க்கும் நாணொடு
நல்லாண்மை என்னும் புணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamak kadumpunal uykkum naanodu
nallaanmai ennum punai.
kurals.meaning: The fierce flood of love sweeps away the raft made of modesty and honourable manliness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you are floating safely on a little raft. Then a huge flood rushes in and carries the raft away. The poet says love is like that flood, and being careful and well-behaved is the raft it sweeps off.
kurals.university: The image is a rūpakam (extended metaphor): kāmak kaṭum-puṉal (காமக் கடும்புனல்), 'the fierce torrent of love', against puṇai (புணை), a raft or float, which here is made of two things, nāṇ (modesty) and nal-āṇmai (honourable manliness), both named in the previous couplet. Uykkum (உய்க்கும்) means 'carries off, drives along'. Commentators (Parimelazhagar's line, Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah) all take it as the hero's explanation of why the qualities he once had could not save him; Puliyur Kesikan adds an exclamation, 'what shall I do!'. Pope: 'Love's rushing tide will sweep away the raft / Of seemly manliness and shame combined.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Just as a strong wind sweeps a boat off its chartered course on the water, even one of the senses on which the mind focuses can lead the intellect astray.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns that a single sense, once the mind follows it, can carry away even a wise person's judgment.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts use the image of a small vessel carried off by a force on the water to describe desire overpowering self-control.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on holy-bhagavad-gita.org; a near one-to-one image, though the Gita warns where the Kural laments.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can the floods drown it.”
christianity.explanation: The Song of Songs says no flood can put out love.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural turns the image around: love is itself the flood, and it is reserve that drowns.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the flood imagery and the invincibility of love match, though the image is inverted.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet is reported to have said that the Fire is surrounded by desires and passions, while Paradise is surrounded by things the self dislikes.
islam.explanation: The hadith teaches that unchecked desire draws a person easily toward harm, while restraint is hard.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's torrent of love sweeping off the raft of restraint shows how easily desire can overpower a person.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a general match on the pull of desire, with a moral judgment the Kural does not make.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud teaches that the evil inclination is at first like a spider's thread and in the end like a cart rope.
judaism.explanation: Rabbinic teaching describes desire as something that starts slight and grows until it holds a person fast.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's 'fierce torrent' is love at the end of that process, when it has grown strong enough to sweep restraint away.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified on Sefaria this session; describes the growing power of desire, but the Talmud's subject is temptation in general, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is no fire like lust; there is no grip like hatred; there is no net like delusion; there is no river like craving.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha names craving as the strongest of rivers, one that carries beings along.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's 'torrent of love' is just such a river, sweeping off the raft of restraint.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; the river image of craving matches closely.

jainism.quote_or_event: “If you fall in love with every woman you see, you will be without hold like the Haṭha-plant, driven before the wind.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati warns Rathanemi that a person carried by desire has no anchor and drifts like a floating water-plant.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's image of restraint swept away by a flood matches this picture of a self driven helplessly by passion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; Jacobi notes the hatha is an aquatic plant, so the water imagery is close.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leander swims the Hellespont every night to reach Hero, guided by her lamp, until one stormy night the waves overwhelm him and he drowns.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Ovid's Heroides and Musaeus' poem, Leander's love drives him into waters that finally carry him off.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural's 'fierce flood' takes literal form in the strait that sweeps the lover away.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known story; flood and lover match, though in the myth the water is literal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle compares the person overcome by passion to someone asleep, mad or drunk, who has knowledge but cannot use it at that moment.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, akrasia (weakness of will) is not ignorance but knowledge swept aside by feeling.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover still knows the worth of modesty, but the torrent of love has carried it away.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard passage; a good analytic match for restraint overwhelmed by passion.

kurals.tamil:
தொடலைக் குறுந்தொடி தந்தாள் மடலொடு
மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thodalaik kurundhodi thandhaal madalodu
maalai uzhakkum thuyar.
kurals.meaning: She who wears small bangles strung like a garland has given me both the palm-stem horse and the sorrow that torments me every evening.
kurals.elementary: Sometimes a person we like very much can make us feel happy and sad at the same time. The speaker says the girl with the pretty little bangles has given him two things: a heavy heart every evening, and the idea of riding the palm horse.
kurals.university: Toṭalaik kuṟun-toṭi (தொடலைக் குறுந்தொடி) is an epithet standing for the heroine: 'she of the small bangles (kuṟun-toṭi) that are like a garland or string (toṭalai)'. Commentators differ on toṭalai: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as 'garland-like, continuous', Kesikan as 'a linked set', while Kalaignar reads in a girdle (mēkalai) as well; Pappaiah's text appears to read 'like a mountain' (malai pōla), probably a misprint for mālai. Mālai uḻakkum tuyar (மாலை உழக்கும் துயர்), 'the sorrow that harrows in the evening', invokes the akam convention that evening is the hardest hour for separated lovers. Pope: 'The maid that slender armlets wears, like flowers entwined, / Has brought me horse of palm, and pangs of eventide!' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In Kalidasa's play, King Dushyanta, after first meeting Shakuntala in the hermitage, grows pale and thin with longing and cannot rest, all because of the girl he has seen.
hinduism.explanation: The love-sickness of the hero is portrayed as caused by a single glimpse of the heroine.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Dushyanta can point to one girl as the source of all his torment.
hinduism.source: Kalidasa, Shakuntala, Act III (paraphrase; cf. tr. Arthur W. Ryder)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the act, not checked word for word this session; a fair fit for love-sickness given by the beloved, without the evening or ornament motifs.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou hast ravished my heart, my sister, my spouse; thou hast ravished my heart with one of thine eyes, with one chain of thy neck.”
christianity.explanation: The lover says that a single glance and a single necklace of the beloved have overpowered his heart.
christianity.tie_back: As the Kural names the beloved by her bangles, the Song names an ornament, a neck-chain, as part of what has undone him.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the ornament detail and the sense of being undone by the beloved match well.

islam.quote_or_event: “When they saw him, they were so stunned ˹by his beauty˺ that they cut their hands.”
islam.explanation: The women of the city, invited to see Joseph, are so overwhelmed by his beauty that they cut their own hands with their knives.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, they suffer pain caused by nothing more than the sight of the beloved's beauty.
islam.source: Qur'an 12:31 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on quran.com; beauty causing pain is a fair match, but the Qur'anic scene is about Joseph's virtue, not shared love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Turn away thine eyes from me, For they have overcome me.”
judaism.explanation: The lover begs the beloved to look away because her eyes overwhelm him.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, he admits that the beloved herself is the source of the power that undoes him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the beloved as the cause of the lover's helplessness fits, without the evening sorrow.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, King Sivi sees the beautiful Ummadanti only once, from a distance, and falls so deeply in love that he grows ill and cannot attend to his duties, though in the end he masters himself.
buddhism.explanation: A single sight of the woman brings the king a sickness of longing that he must overcome.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's speaker also traces his torment to one girl, though in the Jataka the virtue lies in conquering it.
buddhism.source: Ummadanti Jataka (Jataka 527) (paraphrase; cf. tr. E.B. Cowell et al.)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known Jataka; strong on love-sickness given by the beloved's beauty, with a renunciatory ending.

jainism.quote_or_event: On the way to his own wedding, Arishtanemi sees animals penned for the feast, gives his ornaments to his charioteer, and renounces the world, leaving his bride Rajimati in sorrow.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account, one person's decision brings both release for himself and grief for the one who loved him.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's speaker says the beloved 'gave' him sorrow; Rajimati received hers from Arishtanemi in the same way.
jainism.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.14-28 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a passage read on sacred-texts.com this session; only partly parallel, since the Jain story honours the renunciation that causes the grief.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Struck by Cupid's golden arrow, Apollo burns with love for the nymph Daphne, who flees him; the god suffers while she remains untouched until she is changed into a laurel.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows love as a wound inflicted on a lover by forces beyond his control, with the beloved as its focus.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Apollo receives his torment through one maiden who does not share it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; the love-wound fits, but Daphne's refusal and flight go well beyond the Kural.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal describes 'crystallization': the lover's mind keeps covering the beloved with new perfections, so that every small detail about her deepens his attachment and his suffering.
philosophy.explanation: In On Love, the lover's imagination turns ordinary traits into sources of both delight and pain.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover identifies his beloved by a small detail, her little bangles, and blames her for all his sorrow.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not checked this session; a general psychological parallel.

kurals.tamil:
மடலூர்தல் யாமத்தும் உள்ளுவேன் மன்ற
படல்ஒல்லா பேதைக்கென் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Madaloordhal yaamaththum ulluvaen mandra
padalollaa paedhaikken kan.
kurals.meaning: Even at midnight I think about riding the palm-stem horse, for my eyes will not close in sleep because of that innocent girl.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been so worried or excited that you couldn't fall asleep? The speaker lies awake in the middle of the night, thinking about the girl he loves and about his big plan to tell the whole village.
kurals.university: Yāmam (யாமம்) is the deep watch of the night, midnight; uḷḷuvēṉ (உள்ளுவேன்) 'I shall think, brood on', with maṉṟa (மன்ற) 'certainly' as an intensifier. Paṭal ollā (படல் ஒல்லா), 'not consenting to close', describes eyes that will not shut, and pētai (பேதை), literally 'innocent, simple one', is a conventional endearment for the heroine (also a technical term for the youngest of the seven stages of womanhood). Commentators in Parimelazhagar's line take it as the hero assuring the confidante that his resolve is not a passing mood but something he dwells on even at midnight. The ytamizh.com text prints படல்ஒல்லா without a space, thirukkural.net the same; editions vary only in spacing. Pope: 'Of climbing horse of palm in midnight hour, I think; / My eyes know no repose for that same simple maid.'

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, Damayanti, having heard of King Nala's virtues, falls in love with him before they meet; she grows pale and thin, sighs, and loses her rest, so that her companions notice her changed state.
hinduism.explanation: The Nala episode is the classic Sanskrit account of a lover kept awake and wasting through longing.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's lover, Damayanti cannot rest because of the one she loves.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Vana Parva, Nalopakhyana (paraphrase; cf. tr. K.M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, exact verse not checked this session; sleeplessness in love fits, without the madal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved lies awake at night longing for the one she loves.
christianity.tie_back: Both lovers are awake in the night, their thoughts fixed on the beloved.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; close match on night-time longing.

islam.quote_or_event: Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya is remembered as praying through the night, saying that while lovers are alone with their beloveds, she is alone with her Lord.
islam.explanation: The great woman saint of Basra turned the lover's sleepless night into an act of devotion.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's lover is also awake at midnight because of the one he loves; Rabi'a gives that wakefulness a mystical meaning.
islam.source: Farid al-Din 'Attar, Tadhkirat al-Awliya, life of Rabi'a (paraphrase)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a widely cited saying from hagiographic tradition, not verified this session; devotional rather than romantic.

judaism.explanation: The beloved says that even when her body rests, her heart stays awake for the one she loves.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is in the same state: his eyes will not close because his heart is with her.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match on the lover's wakeful heart at night.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha uses the sleepless person's endless night as an image for the long round of existence of those without wisdom.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is that sleepless one, and the Buddhist verse sees his long night as a symptom of attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Access to Insight; shares the sleepless night image but uses it as a metaphor for samsara.

jainism.quote_or_event: Jacobi notes that Rajimati's lament after Arishtanemi's renunciation is the subject of a later Jain Sanskrit poem, the Nemiduta of Vikrama, which borrows the last line of each stanza from Kalidasa's poem of a separated lover, the Meghaduta.
jainism.explanation: Jain poets themselves took up the longing of the abandoned bride as a theme of separation poetry.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's sleepless lover, Rajimati in this tradition is shown dwelling on the beloved who is gone.
jainism.source: Hermann Jacobi, note to Uttaradhyayana Sutra 22.28 (SBE 45), on Vikrama's Nemiduta
jainism._accuracy_note: Based on Jacobi's footnote read on sacred-texts.com; the Nemiduta itself was not consulted, so the match is indirect.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Argonautica, Medea lies awake through the night, torn between shame, which holds her back, and love for Jason, which urges her on to help him against her own father.
greek_mythology.explanation: Apollonius shows a young woman's night-long struggle between modesty and desire.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the heart of the chapter: a lover awake at night, weighing reserve against love.
greek_mythology.source: Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 3 (paraphrase; cf. tr. R.C. Seaton)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; a strong fit on sleeplessness and the shame-versus-love conflict.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And in her madness can neither sleep by night nor abide in her place by day.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates describes the soul of a lover separated from the beautiful one as unable to rest by night or day.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's lover is in exactly this state: his eyes will not close at midnight.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive text of Jowett's translation; a near one-to-one match.

kurals.tamil:
கடலன்ன காமம் உழந்தும் மடலேறாப்
பெண்ணின் பெருந்தக்க தில்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadalanna kaamam uzhandhum madalaeraap
pennin perundhakka thil.
kurals.meaning: There is nothing nobler than a woman who, though she suffers a love as vast as the sea, never rides the palm-stem horse.
kurals.elementary: Imagine two friends who both miss someone very much. One shouts about it all over town; the other keeps going quietly and patiently. The poet says the quiet, patient strength the woman shows is one of the greatest things in the world.
kurals.university: The couplet turns the chapter: kaṭal aṉṉa kāmam (கடலன்ன காமம்), 'love like the sea', is borne (uḻantum, 'even while suffering') by the woman who nonetheless does not ride the madal (maṭal ēṟā). This echoes the Tolkāppiyam rule that the madal is never proper for women, and the commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read it as praise of the endurance of women; Kesikan sharpens it into a comparison: no man has such worth. The speaker is disputed: some commentators give it to the hero, conceding the heroine's greater restraint, while others read it as the heroine's own words, and many hear the remaining couplets of the chapter in her voice. Perun-takkatu il (பெருந்தக்கது இல்) is 'there is nothing of greater worth'. Pope: 'There's nought of greater worth than woman's long-enduring soul, / Who, vexed by love like ocean waves, climbs not the horse of palm.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Held captive in Ravana's Ashoka grove, Sita endures long separation from Rama, refuses every threat and temptation, and keeps her dignity and faith until Hanuman finds her.
hinduism.explanation: The Sundara Kanda makes Sita's quiet endurance in separation the very picture of a noble woman's strength.
hinduism.tie_back: Sita's vast grief borne in dignified restraint is the kind of nobility the Kural praises.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; strong on endurance in separation, though Sita's situation is captivity, not unrequited love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things, endureth all things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes true love as patient endurance that does not give way.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural praises exactly this love that endures all things without breaking out in a public display.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; matches the praise of enduring love, though not specific to women.

islam.quote_or_event: When Jacob hears that Joseph has been lost, he answers that 'beautiful patience' (sabrun jamil) is his course, and he endures his grief with dignity.
islam.explanation: The Qur'an holds up patient, uncomplaining endurance of heartbreak as a mark of nobility.
islam.tie_back: The Kural's woman shows the same 'beautiful patience' in bearing a sea-wide love without display.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; endurance with dignity matches, but the grief is a father's, not a lover's.

judaism.quote_or_event: “She said to him: If he would listen to me, he would sit and study for another twelve years.”
judaism.explanation: Rachel, wife of Rabbi Akiva, endures twelve years of separation and, when mocked as a 'widow of a living man', declares she would bear twelve more for his sake.
judaism.tie_back: Her long, uncomplaining endurance of separation is the kind of nobility the Kural assigns to women.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Ketubot 63a (William Davidson Edition, Sefaria)
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong fit for a woman's patient endurance of separation in love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Buddhist tradition tells that after Prince Siddhartha left home, Yasodhara chose to live as he did, wearing simple robes and eating once a day, enduring her loss with dignity and later becoming a nun.
buddhism.explanation: Yasodhara is remembered for bearing abandonment without bitterness or display.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's woman, Yasodhara bore a great love and loss with restraint.
buddhism.source: Jataka Nidanakatha and later Pali commentarial tradition (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of commentarial tradition rather than early canonical text; matches the theme of dignified endurance.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Firm and decided she cut off her tresses which were black like bees and dressed with a brush and comb.”
jainism.explanation: Forsaken by Arishtanemi, Rajimati does not complain or make a display; she calmly takes up the life of a nun.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural's woman, Rajimati carries a great love with steadiness instead of public protest, though she turns it toward renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong on a woman's composed endurance, though its goal is renunciation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope waits twenty years for Odysseus, putting off the suitors with the trick of the shroud she weaves by day and unravels by night, weeping in private but never giving way.
greek_mythology.explanation: Homer makes her patient, controlled fidelity the model of a noble wife.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Penelope bears a sea of longing without display, as the Kural's woman does.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known episodes; a strong fit for long-suffering, dignified restraint in love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle distinguishes endurance (karteria), the ability to hold out against pains and pressures most people give way to, from softness, which yields.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, enduring what most would not is a mark of strength of character.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural ranks the woman who endures love's sea without yielding to the madal above all others, the same esteem for endurance.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a standard passage; a conceptual parallel without a romantic setting.

kurals.tamil:
நிறையரியர் மன்அளியர் என்னாது காமம்
மறையிறந்து மன்று படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Niraiyariyar manaliyar ennaadhu kaamam
maraiyirandhu mandru padum.
kurals.meaning: Love does not stop to consider whether someone is restrained or deserving of pity; it breaks out of its secrecy and shows itself in the public square.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever tried to keep a happy secret, but your big smile gave it away? Love can be like that. Even when someone tries very hard to hide it, it shows on their face and everyone in town finds out.
kurals.university: The key words are niṟai (நிறை), 'firmness of mind, the power to keep one's feelings in', aḷiyar (அளியர்), 'those deserving pity', maṟai (மறை), 'secrecy', and maṉṟu (மன்று), the village common or public assembly ground where talk spreads. The opening phrase niṟai-ariyar is read in two opposite ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take it as 'lacking restraint', while Solomon Pappaiah reads 'very restrained' (ariyar as 'hard to overcome'), and Pope follows the second ('In virtue hard to move, yet very tender, too, are we'). Pope's 'we' reflects the common view that from here the heroine is speaking, lamenting that her love is about to become public gossip (alar), which leads into chapter 115. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Rukmini, though a modest princess promised by her brother to another, sends a brahmin messenger with a letter to Krishna declaring her love and asking him to carry her away before the wedding.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana praises Rukmini's love for breaking through the reserve expected of her.
hinduism.tie_back: As in the Kural, love refuses to stay hidden in a well-guarded heart and makes itself known.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; love breaking through modesty matches, though Rukmini acts deliberately rather than being betrayed by her feelings.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved openly asks the women of the city to carry word of her love-sickness.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, she finds that her love has passed beyond private feeling into public knowledge.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love made public fits, though here she chooses to tell rather than being exposed.

islam.quote_or_event: “Some women of the city gossiped, ‘The Chief Minister’s wife is trying to seduce her slave-boy. Love for him has plagued her heart.’”
islam.explanation: The Qur'an tells how the Egyptian noblewoman's passion for Joseph became the talk of the city.
islam.tie_back: The verse is a vivid case of the Kural's warning: love breaks out of secrecy and becomes public gossip.
islam.source: Qur'an 12:30 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on quran.com (quotation trimmed); a close match on love becoming public talk, though the Qur'an judges her conduct as wrong.

judaism.quote_or_event: “When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; Yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved wishes her love could be shown openly in the street without bringing scorn.
judaism.tie_back: She feels the same tension as the Kural: love pressing to be seen in public while society watches and judges.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (verse trimmed); a close fit for love wanting to go public under the eyes of others.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha names three things that are carried on in secret rather than in the open, among them affairs with women, and contrasts them with things that shine openly, like the sun, the moon and the Dhamma.
buddhism.explanation: The discourse treats secrecy as a mark of what cannot bear the light.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural observes that love does not stay secret; the Buddhist saying explains why lovers try to keep it so.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase not verified word for word this session; a next-best match on love and secrecy, with a different point.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The daughter of the best king, true to self-control and her vows, maintained the honour of her clan and family, and her virtue, and spoke to him.”
jainism.explanation: Faced with Rathanemi's sudden passion, Rajimati keeps her composure and her family's honour.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural says love ignores a person's restraint and breaks into the open; the Jain text praises a woman whose restraint held firm.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a contrasting ideal rather than a parallel.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides' Hippolytus, Queen Phaedra resolves to hide her love for her stepson in silence and even to starve herself, but her nurse draws the secret from her and it spreads, with tragic results.
greek_mythology.explanation: The play is built around a love that its bearer tries desperately to conceal and cannot.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaedra's story is a tragic form of the Kural's point: love will not stay behind the screen of restraint.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play's plot; a strong fit on love escaping concealment, though Phaedra's love is illicit and tragic.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “There is no disguise which can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.”
philosophy.explanation: La Rochefoucauld observes that real love always shows itself in the end.
philosophy.tie_back: This is almost the Kural's own statement: love breaks through every attempt to keep it hidden.
philosophy.source: François de La Rochefoucauld, Maxims, no. 70 (Project Gutenberg English edition)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the Project Gutenberg text; a near one-to-one match.

kurals.tamil:
அறிகிலார் எல்லாரும் என்றேஎன் காமம்
மறுகின் மறுகும் மருண்டு.
kurals.transliteration:
Arikilaar ellaarum endrae-en kaamam
marukin marukum marundu.
kurals.meaning: As if thinking that not everyone knows of it yet, my love wanders bewildered through the streets.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a puppy that has escaped from its yard and runs up and down the street, bumping into everyone. The speaker says her love is like that: it has got out and is wandering around town where everyone can see it.
kurals.university: Love itself is personified: thinking 'not everyone knows' (aṟikilār ellārum), it maṟukiṉ maṟukum (மறுகின் மறுகும்), 'roams about in the street', maruṇṭu (மருண்டு), 'in confusion, bewildered'. The pun on maṟuku (street) and maṟukum (wanders, whirls) is characteristic of Valluvar's sound-play. Commentators note the irony: because the speaker had kept quiet (Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar: 'because I endured in silence'), love itself seems to have decided to announce itself; Pappaiah says it goes about the streets as gossip (ampal and alar), anticipating chapter 115. The ytamizh.com text prints என்றேஎன் as one unit and thirukkural.net the same; Pope reads 'There's no one knows my heart, so says my love'.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Krishna vanishes from the circle dance, the gopis wander through the forest of Vrindavan as if mad, asking the trees, the creepers and the earth whether they have seen him.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata Purana describes their bewildered search as a sign of love that has taken over their whole being.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's love that roams the streets bewildered, the gopis' love sends them wandering openly in search of the beloved.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode; a strong fit for bewildered, public wandering in love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not.”
christianity.explanation: The beloved leaves her bed and searches the streets of the city for her lover.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural's love wandering the streets in confusion is pictured here almost literally.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match on love wandering the streets.

islam.quote_or_event: “Barira's husband was a slave called Mughith, as if I am seeing him now, going behind Barira and weeping with his tears flowing down his beard.”
islam.explanation: Ibn 'Abbas recalls how Mughith followed Barira through Medina in tears after she left him, and the Prophet remarked on the strength of his love.
islam.tie_back: Mughith's love, like the Kural's, wandered openly through the streets for all to see.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com; a close match on love displayed in public streets.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved goes out at night calling for her lover and cannot find him.
judaism.tie_back: Her calling and searching through the city is the same restless, public wandering the Kural gives to love.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (verse trimmed); strong on searching, though the street setting is in the next verse.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Kisa Gotami, grief-stricken at her child's death, carries him from house to house through the town asking for medicine, while people think she has lost her mind, until the Buddha gently leads her to understanding.
buddhism.explanation: The commentarial story shows how attachment can send a person wandering bewildered in public.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural's love, her attachment drives her through the streets in confusion for all to see.
buddhism.source: Therigatha commentary, story of Kisa Gotami (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a commentarial story; the bewildered public wandering matches, but the attachment is a mother's grief, not romantic love.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Sutrakritanga warns monks that one who gives way to infatuation with a woman loses the respect he had and ends up mocked and ordered about, his weakness known to all.
jainism.explanation: The chapter on women in this early Jain text describes how desire, once yielded to, becomes a public humiliation.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural describes love becoming public; the Jain text treats that exposure as a warning.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the chapter's general argument, not verified this session; a next-best match written from a monastic and disapproving angle.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: After losing Eurydice a second time, Orpheus wanders grieving through the wild lands of Thrace, refusing all other love and singing of his loss.
greek_mythology.explanation: Virgil and Ovid show love that has lost its object and roams openly in its sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's bewildered love wandering the streets, Orpheus' love wanders openly with nowhere to rest.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known passages; wandering love fits, though Orpheus grieves a death rather than unrevealed love.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza remarks that people who are inflamed with love and dream night and day of nothing but their beloved are, like the greedy and the ambitious, in a kind of madness, though people do not usually call it so.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, an emotion that fixes the mind on one object takes away its freedom.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural's love, wandering bewildered through the streets, is that kind of mind-possessing passion made visible.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from memory, not verified this session; a reasonable analytic parallel.

kurals.tamil:
யாம்கண்ணின் காண நகுப அறிவில்லார்
யாம்பட்ட தாம்படா ஆறு.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaamkannin kaana nagupa arivillaar
yaampatta thaampadaa aaru.
kurals.meaning: Thoughtless people laugh at me right before my eyes, only because they have never suffered what I suffer.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever seen someone laugh at a friend who was crying, just because they didn't understand how sad the friend felt? The speaker says people who laugh at lovers only do it because they have never felt that pain themselves.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on a balanced contrast: yām paṭṭa (யாம் பட்ட), 'what I have suffered', against tām paṭā (தாம் படா), 'what they have not suffered', with āṟu (ஆறு), 'the manner, the reason', at the end. Aṟivillār (அறிவில்லார்), 'those without understanding', laugh kaṇṇiṉ kāṇa (கண்ணின் காண), 'so that I see it with my eyes', that is, openly to the speaker's face. Commentators take it as the closing lament of the chapter, spoken in the tradition as the heroine's words once her love is known, and Kalaignar turns it into a general maxim: only those who have never known love's pain mock its sufferers. Pope: 'Before my eyes the foolish make a mock of me, / Because they ne'er endured the pangs I now must drie.' The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In her songs, the princess-poet Mirabai says that people call her mad and that she has thrown away family honour and public shame (lok-laj) for love of Krishna, and she accepts their mockery.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti tradition preserves Mira's defiant answer to the scorn of her in-laws and her town.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, Mira is laughed at by those who have never felt the love that has seized her.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, padas (paraphrase; cf. tr. A.J. Alston, The Devotional Poems of Mirabai, 1980)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of recurring themes in Mira's songs, specific pada not identified; a close fit for being mocked for love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Others mocking said, These men are full of new wine.”
christianity.explanation: At Pentecost, onlookers who did not understand what had seized the apostles mocked them as drunk.
christianity.tie_back: As in the Kural, people who have not shared an overwhelming experience laugh at those who have.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the pattern of mockery from the uncomprehending fits, but the experience is spiritual, not romantic.

islam.quote_or_event: “This is the one for whose love you criticized me!”
islam.explanation: After the women of the city have seen Joseph for themselves and been overwhelmed, the noblewoman answers their earlier gossip.
islam.tie_back: Her retort makes the Kural's point: those who mock a lover change their tune once they have felt the same thing.
islam.source: Qur'an 12:32 (tr. Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on quran.com (verse trimmed); a close structural match, though the Qur'an condemns her pursuit of Joseph.

judaism.quote_or_event: When David dances with all his might before the Ark, Michal mocks him for shamelessly uncovering himself, and he answers: “And I will be yet more vile than thus, and will be base in mine own sight.”
judaism.explanation: David refuses to be shamed out of his joyous, undignified devotion by someone who does not share it.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, David is mocked for abandoning reserve by one who has not felt what moves him.
judaism._accuracy_note: Quoted words verified verbatim on Sefaria; the pattern fits well, but David's love is for God, not a beloved.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha tells Atula that people have always blamed others: they blame the one who sits silent, the one who speaks much, and the one who speaks little; there is no one in the world who is not blamed.
buddhism.explanation: The verse teaches that ridicule from others says more about the world than about the one ridiculed.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is laughed at too; the Dhammapada advises not to measure oneself by such mockery.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not checked word for word this session; a next-best match on unjust mockery.

jainism.quote_or_event: The Acaranga recounts that during Mahavira's wanderings in the rough Ladha country people struck him, set dogs on him and abused him, and he bore it all without anger.
jainism.explanation: Mahavira's calm under the scorn and violence of those who did not understand him is a model of Jain forbearance.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural's lover is mocked by those who have not shared his experience; Mahavira shows a Jain answer to such ridicule, patient endurance.
jainism.source: Acaranga Sutra 1.8.3 (paraphrase; tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase, not verified this session; a next-best match on enduring mockery, with nothing about love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Hephaestus traps Ares and Aphrodite in his net, he calls the gods to see, and they break into unquenchable laughter at the lovers.
greek_mythology.explanation: The bard Demodocus' song in the Odyssey shows lovers exposed to the laughter of onlookers.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural's speaker, the lovers are laughed at openly once their love is known, though in Homer the laughter has more justification.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode; a next-best match, since the lovers are adulterers rather than sympathetic sufferers.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “As he forgets earthly interests and is rapt in the divine, the vulgar deem him mad, and rebuke him; they do not see that he is inspired.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says the person seized by the divine madness of love is mocked by ordinary people who do not understand it.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural's complaint exactly: those without understanding laugh at a lover because they have not felt what he feels.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on the MIT Internet Classics Archive text of Jowett's translation; strong match, though Plato's lover is a lover of the divine beauty, not only a human one.
